Remove all the crowd noise with strong noise reduction.
The interview loses its place and sounds artificial.
Add a quick fade out and fade in at every single cut.
Fades make the noise dip at each cut.
Lower the crowd noise on all shots to the same level.
A matching level doesn't remove the jumps.
I10.why: A continuous layer of crowd sound hides the jumps, so the cuts feel smooth and the place feels real.

I10.q: An NGO hires you for a short film about a farmer struggling after a drought. The client sends an upbeat dance track to use. What do you do?
options: Suggest a slower, gentler track and explain why it suits the story.
Use the dance track as it is, since the client picked it.
The music works against the story; the client needs advice.
Use the dance track but keep it very low in the mix.
Quiet upbeat music still sends the wrong mood.
Slow the dance track down until it feels gentler.
Slowing it changes its pitch and doesn't make the mood right.
I10.why: Music tells viewers how to feel. Part of your job is to guide clients toward music that supports their message.

I10.q: In Curtis Judd's demonstration, how does the music behave while someone is speaking?
options: It stays clearly quieter than the voice but never fully disappears.
It plays at about the same level as the voice to add energy.
Equal levels make the voice hard to understand.
It is switched off completely every time anyone says a word.
Switching off completely makes the sound jump in and out.
It fades out slowly and returns only after the speech is finished.
The music should stay under the speech, not leave.
I10.why: The music stays present but clearly underneath, so it supports the scene without covering the dialogue.
I10.video: Mix music behind dialogue — Sound for Video Session

I10.q: You make a phone reel at a dosa stall. The sizzle when batter hits the hot tawa was not captured well. What do you do?
options: Add a clean sizzle sound, timed to the moment the batter lands.
Add a dramatic whoosh sound as the batter is poured.
A whoosh doesn't match what viewers see.
Leave that part silent and let the music carry it.
Silence loses the sound that sells the dosa.
Add a sizzle that plays for the whole length of the clip.
The sizzle should happen when the batter lands.
I10.why: A real sound that matches the action, in perfect sync, makes the image feel solid and appetising.

I10.q: You add a door-closing sound to a scene in a small office. It sounds fake. What is the most likely reason?
options: It is louder than the scene and has none of the room's echo.
It needs more bass so it feels heavier and more real.
Bass doesn't make it fit the room.
It should be spread wide across left and right speakers.
Spreading wide doesn't match a door in one spot.
It needs a higher pitch so it sounds more like a real door.
Pitch isn't the problem; level and room echo are.
I10.why: Effects must match the level and echo of the place on screen. Lower it and add a little room sound so it blends.

I10.q: dB (decibels) measures loudness. In a wedding film, the father's speech peaks around -12 dB and the music around -14 dB. What do you change?
options: Bring the music down to around -24 dB under the speech.
Raise the speech to 0 dB so it sits above the music.
Going to 0 dB risks distortion.
Leave both, since viewers can turn up the volume.
The speech won't be clear for a viewer who can't turn it up.
Lower the speech to -24 dB so it blends with the music.
The speech should stay the strongest sound.
I10.why: The speech should lead, with music roughly 10 dB or more below it, so every word comes through.

I10.q: In the Adobe workshop with John Knowles, why are dialogue, music and effects kept on separate tracks?
options: So each type of sound can be set and adjusted on its own.
So the final video file exports faster from the editor.
Tracks don't change export speed.
So one volume setting can be applied to every sound.
The point is to adjust each type separately.
So the sound stays in sync when the clips are moved.
Separate tracks don't keep sync; they keep control.
I10.why: Separate tracks let you shape the speech first, then place music and effects underneath it on purpose.

I10.q: Your mix for a small business ad sounds perfect on good headphones. What should you do before delivering it?
options: Play it on a phone speaker and cheap earphones to check it.
Boost the whole mix a little so it sounds stronger.
Boosting can cause distortion.
Deliver it, since good headphones show the true sound.
Most viewers don't use good headphones.
Check it on a second pair of good headphones.
You need to hear it as viewers do, on small speakers.
I10.why: Checking on the devices your audience uses shows whether the speech stays clear above the music.

I10.q: In the RX 11 video, what do you compare before putting the repaired dialogue back?
options: Clarity, artefacts and how much natural room sound is left.
Only the loudness.
Loudness alone doesn't show if the voice sounds natural.
Nothing. Repaired audio is always better.
Repair can leave artefacts.
Only whether the hiss is gone.
A clean-sounding clip can still sound unnatural.
I10.why: Fix, compare and keep it natural.
I10.video: Remove Background Noise with RX 11 + Audio Post-production Tips

I10.q: You remove all the echo from a voice recorded in a big hall. Now it sounds like a different room from the pictures. What do you do?
options: Leave a little room sound so it matches what viewers see.
Remove the echo from every clip.
That would make the whole film sound dead.
Add music over it.
Music doesn't match the voice to the room.
Add heavy reverb so it sounds like the hall again.
Too much reverb sounds artificial.
I10.why: Sound should match the space on screen.

I11.q: You made a warm look on a mehendi clip shot by a window. You paste it onto a clip shot under yellow bulbs, and that clip turns far too orange. What do you do?
options: Correct the second clip's white balance and brightness first, then paste the same look.
Lower the strength of the look on the second clip until it seems right.
The mismatch comes from the clip, not the look.
Build a separate new look for the second clip from scratch.
Two different looks won't match each other.
Paste the look and fix the orange with the saturation slider.
Lowering saturation is a rough fix that leaves a muddy cast.
I11.why: One look gives the same result only when clips start from a similar, neutral base. Correct each clip on its own, then the shared look works on both.

I11.q: You put a LUT (a preset file that gives a colour look) on a shop promo clip that was shot too dark. Now it looks muddy. What is the best fix?
options: Take the LUT off, correct the clip underneath, then put the LUT back on.
Try a stronger LUT so the new look covers the muddy areas.
A stronger LUT makes it worse.
Keep the LUT and add sharpening so the clip looks cleaner.
Sharpening doesn't fix the colour or brightness.
Brighten the clip after the LUT so it stops looking muddy.
A LUT expects correct footage before it is added.
I11.why: A LUT expects a normal starting image. If the clip is wrong underneath, correct that first and the LUT will look as intended.

I11.q: You are editing on a laptop in a sunny room. A face looks fine to you, but the waveform shows it sitting very low. What do you do?
options: Go by the waveform and lift the face, since the bright room changes how the screen looks.
Leave it as it is, because it looks fine on your screen right now.
A bright room fools your eyes.
Turn your laptop brightness up until the face looks bright enough.
That changes your screen, not your footage.
Check it on your phone in the same sunny room and trust it.
The phone is fooled by the bright room too.
I11.why: A waveform measures the real brightness of the video. Your view depends on your screen and room, which can mislead you.

I11.q: In the Adobe correction and grading demonstration, what are the colour controls used for across the sequence?
options: To correct each shot and make the shots look consistent with each other.
To give each shot its own different creative look for variety.
That is grading; first correct and match.
To push saturation up so all the footage looks more lively.
Saturation alone doesn't correct anything.
To apply the final creative look to the entire film.
That comes after correction.
I11.why: The video shows correction and matching as the main job of the colour tools, so the sequence plays as one smooth piece.

I11.q: You filmed a shopkeeper interview with two cameras. Camera B looks bluer and slightly darker than camera A. What do you do?
options: Adjust camera B to match camera A, comparing frames of the same face.
Leave it, since viewers accept that each angle looks a bit different.
Viewers see a colour change at each cut.
Make both cameras much warmer so the blue difference is hidden.
Warming both leaves the mismatch.
Match camera B to camera A by eye using the whole frame.
Use the face, which viewers judge most.
I11.why: When you cut between angles, both should feel like the same room and moment. Comparing the same face gives a clear reference.

I11.q: In the Adobe video, what does the Color Match tool do?
options: It compares a shot with a reference shot and adjusts it to match.
It adds a ready-made film look to every clip at the same time.
That is a LUT or preset.
It sets the brightest and darkest points of a single shot.
That is setting black and white points, not matching.
It copies the white balance setting from the camera into the editor.
Color Match works on the footage, not the camera settings.
I11.why: Color Match uses a neighbouring or reference image as a target, then shifts the colour of your shot towards it.
I11.video: Create a professional look using Color Match and Curves

I11.q: At a family function lit by tube lights, your aunt's face looks slightly greenish. What is the best fix?
options: Move the tint a little towards magenta while watching the faces.
Raise saturation so her face looks more colourful and alive.
More colour makes the green stronger.
Warm the whole shot strongly until the green is gone.
A strong warm shift changes the whole look.
Cool the whole shot so the green blends into blue.
Cooling moves further from natural skin.
I11.why: Tint controls the green to magenta balance. A small move towards magenta cancels the green that tube lights often add.

I11.q: You use a vectorscope (a scope that shows which way colours lean and how strong they are) to check skin. What should you look for?
options: Skin sitting near the skin tone guide line, whatever the person's complexion.
Skin pulled to the centre so it shows almost no colour at all.
Skin should keep its natural colour.
Darker skin moved away from the line to make it look fairer.
The line is the same for every complexion.
Skin pulled out to the edge to make it vivid.
Over-saturated skin looks unnatural.
I11.why: Skin of every complexion falls close to one guide line on the vectorscope. Only brightness differs, so the line is a reliable check.

I11.q: For a small bakery ad, you add a strong teal look you love. Now the cakes look grey-blue. What do you do?
options: Ease the look back so the cakes keep their real, tasty colours.
Keep it strong, since bold looks make ads feel modern.
Food that looks grey-blue puts people off.
Use the look on only some shots to add some variety.
Shots would no longer match.
Raise saturation on the whole video to bring the cakes back.
That also boosts the teal.
I11.why: The grade should help sell the cakes. A gentle look keeps the food appealing and keeps attention on the product.

I11.q: Your log footage (a flat recording mode that keeps more detail) looks washed out. Following the Color Management video, what should you do first?
options: Set how the software reads the footage's colour, so it displays correctly.
Add any LUT that looks good and adjust things from there.
A LUT on wrongly read footage gives wrong colour.
Raise contrast and saturation by hand until it looks right.
That is guesswork and may break the footage.
Turn the footage to black and white and add colour back.
That throws away the colour you need.
I11.why: The video explains that correct input and colour management settings show the footage properly before any creative work.

I12.q: You add a white title over a shot of a bright sky at a wedding venue. On your phone, the words almost vanish. What do you do?
options: Add a soft dark shadow or band behind the words
Make the white letters thinner and more stylish
Thin letters vanish even more against a bright sky.
Leave it, since viewers can pause the video
Viewers shouldn't have to pause to read a title.
Change the title colour to light yellow
Light yellow on a bright sky is still low contrast.
I12.why: White on a bright sky has almost no contrast. A shadow or dark band separates the words from the background so they stand out.

I12.q: Your end card for a tailor shop shows the address and phone number. It sits near the bottom corner and lasts one second. What do you change?
options: Move it in from the edges and hold it for about four seconds
Keep the spot but use a fancier script font for style
A fancy font is harder to read in the time you give it.
Keep the timing but make the letters smaller and neater
Smaller letters are harder to read.
Move it to the middle of the screen and hold it for 10 seconds
That covers the picture and holds far longer than needed.
I12.why: Text near the edge can be cut off or hidden by app buttons. Viewers need a few seconds to read a number, ideally twice.

I12.q: You are editing a family function film. The bride's aunt, Meena Iyer, gives a short speech. Which on-screen title do you use?
options: Meena Iyer, Bride's Aunt
Meena
A first name alone doesn't say who she is.
Meena Iyer, who came from Chennai to bless the couple
Too long to read while she speaks.
Aunt Meena
It doesn't give her full name or whose aunt she is.
I12.why: A full name plus one short role tells the viewer everything they need, fast.

I12.q: A client wants their owner's title to read: "Ravi Kumar, Founder, CEO, Master Chef and Award Winner since 2005". What do you suggest?
options: Pick the one role that matters most for this video
Keep every role but shrink the font to make it fit
A tiny font is hard to read on a phone.
Keep every role and split it over three lines
Three lines of titles crowd the picture.
Keep the first two roles and cut the rest
Two roles are still too many; pick the one that matters here.
I12.why: One clear role is easy to read. Extra details can go in the voiceover or description.

I12.q: You watch back your captions on an interview. Each line appears about one second before the person starts saying it. What do you do?
options: Shift each line so it starts when the voice starts
Leave it, since early captions give more reading time
Captions that lead the voice confuse viewers.
Make every line longer so the gap is less noticeable
